statement: Ivy draws a house: a square with a triangle roof sitting exactly on its top side. The roof's two slanted sides are equal. How many lines of symmetry does the house have?

choices.misconception: I thought a line straight across the middle works too, because it works for the square.
I thought the roof has 3 lines of symmetry, like a triangle with all sides equal.
I counted the lines of symmetry of the square and forgot the roof.
I added the 4 lines of the square and 3 lines for the triangle.

hints: Picture folding the whole house, roof and all.
A line of symmetry must work for the whole shape at once. Try each line that works for the square and check whether the roof matches on both sides of it too.
Fold the house straight down the middle, through the top of the roof. Now try folding across the middle, or corner to corner. Does the roof land on itself?

solutions.reliable: A fold straight down the middle goes through the tip of the roof. The two slanted sides are equal, so the halves match. A fold across the middle would put the roof onto the bottom of the square, which has no roof, so it fails. Corner-to-corner folds also move the roof onto a side of the square. So there is exactly 1 line of symmetry. The idea to keep: a line of symmetry must work for every part of the shape.

whyOnTest: Adding a piece to a shape can destroy symmetry, and students who count the lines of each part separately fall into the trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
